venetian-modon-and-coron.t: Twin Venetian fortress ports at the south-western tip of the Peloponnese, known as the eyes of the Republic, which guarded Venice's route to the Levant for three centuries.
venetian-modon-and-coron.o: Venice claimed the south-western Peloponnese in the partition of the Byzantine Empire after 1204. Venetian forces occupied Modon (Methoni) and Coron (Koroni) around 1207, and the Treaty of Sapienza with Geoffrey I of Villehardouin of the Principality of Achaea confirmed them in 1209.
venetian-modon-and-coron.r: The two ports were governed by Venetian castellans and officials appointed from Venice, and served as stopovers for merchant galleys and pilgrim ships bound for the Holy Land and the eastern Mediterranean. Their surroundings produced wine, silk and food for the fleets, and they gathered news about the Aegean, hence their nickname. Greek, Jewish and Albanian communities lived under Venetian rule.
venetian-modon-and-coron.e: In 1500, during the Ottoman-Venetian war, Sultan Bayezid II stormed Modon after a long siege, and Coron surrendered soon after. Venice briefly regained them in 1686-1715 as part of the Venetian Morea. The fortress of Methoni still stands.

vulci.t: Wealthy Etruscan city near the Fiora river whose tombs held thousands of Greek vases and whose François Tomb preserves an Etruscan version of early Roman history.
vulci.o: Vulci, Etruscan Velch, grew from Villanovan villages on a plateau above the Fiora river, some 10 km from the coast. By the 7th and 6th centuries BCE it had become one of the richest cities of Etruria, importing luxury goods and controlling a large territory reaching towards Lake Bolsena.
vulci.r: Vulci was a major centre of bronze-working, exporting tripods, vessels and candelabra across Italy and beyond the Alps. Its tombs yielded an extraordinary number of Athenian painted vases, many excavated by Lucien Bonaparte in the 19th century. The François Tomb's paintings show the Vulcian heroes Caile and Avle Vipinas and Macstrna, whom the emperor Claudius identified with Rome's king Servius Tullius.
vulci.e: Rome defeated Vulci together with Volsinii in 280 BCE, when Tiberius Coruncanius celebrated a triumph over both. Much of its coastal land was confiscated and the Latin colony of Cosa founded there in 273 BCE. The city declined into a minor Roman town and was abandoned in the early Middle Ages.

vasates.t: Aquitanian people south of the Garonne whose town Cossium became Bazas, centre of the Bazadais.
vasates.o: The Vasates, called Vocates by Caesar, lived south of the middle Garonne in the modern Gironde. They surrendered to Publius Crassus in 56 BCE with the other Aquitanian peoples.
vasates.r: No rulers or institutions are known. Their territory lay between the Garonne valley and the Landes forest, on the route from Burdigala to the Pyrenees.
vasates.e: Under Rome their chief town Cossium was renamed Civitas Vasatica, from which comes Bazas. The poet Ausonius had family links with the town, and its district kept the name Bazadais.

venetian-nauplia.t: Venetian-ruled port of Nauplia, called Napoli di Romania, a fortified base in the Argolid for a century and a half.
venetian-nauplia.o: In 1388 Marie of Enghien, heiress of the Lordship of Argos and Nauplia, sold her lands to Venice. The Byzantine despot Theodore I seized Argos first, but returned it to Venice in 1394. Nauplia, which the Venetians called Napoli di Romania, became the centre of Venetian rule in the eastern Peloponnese.
venetian-nauplia.r: Venetian officials governed from Nauplia, strengthening the walls of the Acronauplia and building the harbour fort of Bourtzi in 1471. The town traded grain, wine and silk and hosted Greek, Albanian and Italian communities; Albanian soldiers (stradioti) served Venice. Argos was lost to the Ottomans in 1463, leaving Nauplia an outpost surrounded by Ottoman territory.
venetian-nauplia.e: After the Ottoman-Venetian war of 1537-1540, Venice surrendered Nauplia and Monemvasia to the Ottomans under the peace treaty of 1540. Venice returned in 1686 during the creation of the Venetian Morea.

venetian-morea.t: The Peloponnese under Venice after Morosini's conquest in 1685-1687, a brief reform-minded colony that collapsed in the Ottoman reconquest of 1715.
venetian-morea.o: In the Morean War, part of the Great Turkish War, the Venetian commander Francesco Morosini conquered the Peloponnese between 1685 and 1687; during his campaign in Attica a Venetian shell exploded the Parthenon. The Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 confirmed Venetian possession of the Morea as the Kingdom of the Morea.
venetian-morea.r: Venice divided the peninsula into four provinces under a provveditore generale at Nauplia, carried out a detailed census and land register, and settled colonists to revive a depopulated, war-damaged land. It favoured the Catholic church, which irritated the Orthodox majority, and built the great fortress of Palamidi above Nauplia in 1711-1714.
venetian-morea.e: The Ottomans attacked in 1715 and took the whole Morea within a few months, helped by weak garrisons and the indifference of the Greeks. The Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 confirmed the Ottoman reconquest.

viye-kingdom.t: An Ovimbundu kingdom of the Bie plateau whose traders carried goods across Central Africa, and whose defeat in 1890 opened the interior to Portugal.
viye-kingdom.o: Viye (Bie) was founded by the 18th century, tradition says by a hunter named Viye, on the eastern edge of the Angolan central highlands. Like the Bailundo Kingdom, it grew as a raiding and trading state supplying captives to Benguela.
viye-kingdom.r: Viye's kings ruled from a fortified capital through titled officials. Ovimbundu caravans from Viye travelled to the Lunda lands, the upper Zambezi and Katanga, trading in slaves, ivory, beeswax and later rubber. The Portuguese trader Antonio da Silva Porto lived at Belmonte in Viye for decades and led trading expeditions into the interior.
viye-kingdom.e: In 1890 King Ndunduma expelled a Portuguese expedition, and Silva Porto died after the confrontation. Portugal sent a punitive force that defeated Ndunduma and exiled him, bringing Viye into Portuguese Angola. The town of Kuito grew on its lands.

veii.t: The richest Etruscan city near Rome, its great rival for three centuries until Marcus Furius Camillus captured it in 396 BCE after a ten-year siege.
veii.o: Veii stood on a defended tufa plateau about 16 km north of Rome, and grew from several Villanovan villages that merged into one large settlement by the 8th century BCE. It controlled the right bank of the Tiber and the salt and trade routes that Rome also wanted, making conflict between the two almost inevitable.
veii.r: Veii was famed for its craftsmen: the terracotta statues of the Portonaccio temple, including the Apollo of Veii, are among the finest Etruscan works, and Roman tradition credited a Veientine sculptor, Vulca, with the cult statue of Jupiter on the Capitol. Its territory had dense rural settlement and a sophisticated system of drainage tunnels. It was ruled by kings, notably Lars Tolumnius in the late 5th century.
veii.e: Rome and Veii fought repeatedly over Fidenae and the Tiber crossing. In 396 BCE, after a siege said to have lasted ten years, Camillus took the city, reportedly by tunnelling under its walls. Its land was divided among Roman citizens, doubling Rome's territory, and the city never recovered as an independent power.

viscounty-of-narbonne.t: The viscounty of the old Roman port of Narbonne, famed under Viscountess Ermengard as a centre of troubadour culture and Mediterranean trade.
viscounty-of-narbonne.o: Viscounts appear at Narbonne around 900 as deputies of the counts of Toulouse, who had inherited authority over the former Carolingian march of Septimania. The office became hereditary, and the viscounts shared power in the city with its powerful archbishops.
viscounty-of-narbonne.r: Narbonne was a busy port and a centre of Jewish learning. Viscountess Ermengard, who ruled from 1134 to 1192, presided over a court celebrated by troubadours and steered between Toulouse and Barcelona. Later viscounts survived the Albigensian Crusade by siding with the crusaders, while the river's shift and the silting of the port slowly cut the city's trade.
viscounty-of-narbonne.e: The viscounty passed to the house of Foix in the 15th century. In 1507 Gaston de Foix exchanged it with his uncle Louis XII for the duchy of Nemours, and it was joined to the Kingdom of France.
ru: Gaston de Foix, Duke of Nemours

volcae-arecomici.t: Celtic people of eastern Languedoc whose sacred spring at Nemausus became the Roman city of Nîmes.
volcae-arecomici.o: The Arecomici were the eastern branch of the Volcae, a Celtic people who settled between the Rhône and the Hérault in the 3rd century BCE. Strabo records that twenty-four villages were subject to their chief town Nemausus, which grew up around a sacred spring.
volcae-arecomici.r: They lived in hilltop oppida such as Nages and Mont Vaucluse, and Nemausus had a stone tower, the Tour Magne, before the Romans arrived. They traded closely with Massalia and struck coins with Greek and Latin letters.
volcae-arecomici.e: Their land came under Rome in 121 BCE and part of it was given to Massalia by Pompey. Nemausus became a Latin colony with rich monuments, including the Maison Carrée and the aqueduct carried by the Pont du Gard.

volsinii.t: Leading Etruscan city whose shrine of Voltumna was the religious heart of the Etruscan League, crushed by Rome in 264 BCE after a slave uprising.
volsinii.o: Volsinii, Etruscan Velzna, grew on the volcanic plateau of modern Orvieto from Villanovan settlements of the early 1st millennium BCE. By the 6th century BCE it was a wealthy city with orderly necropolises such as Crocifisso del Tufo, where tombs were laid out in streets and inscribed with owners' names.
volsinii.r: Volsinii controlled a rich territory around Lake Bolsena and traded widely, as imported Greek pottery shows. Nearby lay the Fanum Voltumnae, the federal sanctuary where the twelve Etruscan peoples met each year for games, cult and council. The city was governed by an aristocracy; ancient sources say it was so rich that Rome took some 2,000 statues as booty from it.
volsinii.e: After wars with Rome in the 4th and early 3rd centuries, Volsinii's aristocrats asked Rome for help when freedmen and former slaves seized power. Rome besieged and destroyed the city in 264 BCE and moved survivors to Volsinii Novi, modern Bolsena. Rome also transferred the cult of Vertumnus to the Aventine.

viscounty-of-bearn.t: Pyrenean lordship that made itself a sovereign state under Gaston Fébus and gave France its king Henry IV.
viscounty-of-bearn.o: Béarn emerged in the 9th century as a viscounty within the Duchy of Gascony, ruled by a family later called the Centulles from Lescar and then Morlaàs. Gaston IV took part in the First Crusade and helped Aragon conquer Zaragoza in 1118. The seat later moved to Orthez and, from 1464, to Pau.
viscounty-of-bearn.r: The Fors de Béarn guaranteed local liberties, and the viscount had to swear to respect them. Gaston III, called Fébus, refused homage to both France and England in 1347 and ruled Béarn as a sovereign land; he also wrote a famous treatise on hunting. Through marriages the viscounts became counts of Foix and kings of Navarre.
viscounty-of-bearn.e: Queen Jeanne d'Albret made Calvinism the official religion in the 1560s. Her son Henry, born at Pau, became Henry IV of France in 1589, but Béarn stayed separate until Louis XIII annexed it in 1620 and restored Catholicism.

volsci.t: Italic people of southern Latium who raided and fought Rome for two centuries, the enemies of the legendary Coriolanus.
volsci.o: The Volsci spoke an Osco-Umbrian language and appear in the late 6th century BCE moving from the Apennines into the Lepini mountains, the Liri valley and the Pontine plain. They took over existing Latin towns such as Velitrae, Satricum and Antium, and Anxur (Tarracina) on the coast.
volsci.r: The Volsci formed a loose group of towns rather than a unified state, cooperating in war, often alongside the Aequi. Antium was a port with a fleet that raided the coast. Their language is known chiefly from a bronze tablet from Velitrae. Roman legend made them the people among whom the exiled Gnaeus Marcius Coriolanus took refuge before leading them against Rome.
volsci.e: Wars with Rome and the Latins continued through the 5th and 4th centuries BCE. After the Latin War Rome took Antium in 338 BCE and displayed the beaks (rostra) of its warships in the Forum. Privernum fell in 329 BCE and Sora in the following decades, and by about 304 BCE the Volsci had been absorbed.

veronese-league.t: A short-lived alliance of Veneto cities against Frederick Barbarossa's officials, and the forerunner of the Lombard League.
veronese-league.o: In 1164 Verona, Vicenza, Padua and Treviso, with the backing of the Republic of Venice and the Byzantine Empire, formed a league to resist the taxes and officials imposed by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa in northern Italy.
veronese-league.r: The league was a sworn alliance of independent communes rather than a state. Its members promised mutual defence and refused imperial demands, and Barbarossa failed to subdue them in 1164. Venice supplied money and diplomatic support, eager to keep the emperor out of the Adriatic hinterland.
veronese-league.e: In 1167 the Veronese League merged with the Lombard cities to form the much larger Lombard League, which defeated Barbarossa at Legnano in 1176.

vennicnii.t: People of north-west Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, near a headland he called Vennicnium in modern Donegal.
vennicnii.o: The Vennicnii are known only from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which places them on the north-western coast of Ireland, with a headland named Vennicnium Promontorium, usually identified with Bloody Foreland or another point on the Donegal coast. His Irish information came from earlier sailors' reports.
vennicnii.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or customs. The rugged coastline and uplands of Donegal supported small farming and fishing communities, and later stone forts such as the Grianan of Aileach show the importance of hilltop centres in the region.
vennicnii.e: No later source mentions the Vennicnii. Donegal later became the territory of the northern Uí Néill dynasties, including the Cenél Conaill and the rulers of the Kingdom of Ailech.

vaccaei.t: A Celtic people of the Douro plains famed for sharing out land and harvests collectively, who resisted Rome until the 1st century BCE.
vaccaei.o: The Vaccaei occupied the middle Douro valley, in modern Valladolid, Palencia, Zamora and Burgos, from about the 4th century BCE. Their towns included Intercatia, Pallantia, Cauca and Pintia.
vaccaei.r: Diodorus records that they divided their land each year by lot, pooled the harvest and gave each family its share, punishing hoarding with death. They lived in large towns on the open cereal plains, and the cemetery of Las Ruedas at Pintia shows a warrior elite. They spoke a Celtic language.
vaccaei.e: Hannibal raided them in 220 BCE. In 151 BCE Lucullus massacred the people of Cauca, and later Pallantia withstood several Roman sieges. The Vaccaei fought on into the 1st century BCE, last rising in 56 BCE, before being absorbed into Hispania Citerior.

venetian-crete.t: Venice's most important overseas colony for over four centuries, where Greek and Italian culture blended to produce El Greco and the Cretan Renaissance.
venetian-crete.o: After the Fourth Crusade, Venice bought the claim to Crete from Boniface of Montferrat in 1204. The Genoese adventurer Enrico Pescatore occupied the island first, and Venice only took control around 1211-1212, sending colonists who received land in return for military service. The capital, Candia, gave its name to the colony.
venetian-crete.r: A Venetian duke and councillors governed, and Venetian settlers formed a feudal nobility over a Greek Orthodox peasantry whose church was subordinated to Latin bishops. Frequent revolts, including the Revolt of Saint Titus of 1363, were crushed. Crete exported wine (malmsey), oil and grain. In the 16th century Greek-Italian culture flourished: the Cretan school of icon painting, El Greco and the romance Erotokritos.
venetian-crete.e: The Ottomans invaded in 1645 and besieged Candia for more than twenty years, one of the longest sieges in history. Candia surrendered in 1669, ending Venetian rule except for a few island forts.

vaiga.t: Ancient Estonian district on the western shore of Lake Peipus, contested between Novgorod and the Livonian crusaders.
vaiga.o: Vaiga, called Waiga in Latin sources, lay north of Tartu between the Emajõgi river and Lake Peipus. It is known from Henry of Livonia's chronicle as one of the smaller Estonian lands of the early 13th century.
vaiga.r: Its people farmed and fished on the lake shore and were exposed to Rus' influence; Novgorod and Pskov raided and levied tribute in the area. Some inhabitants accepted Orthodox baptism before Latin missionaries arrived. Its elders are not named in the sources.
vaiga.e: Vaiga was conquered by the crusaders in the campaigns of 1220-1224 and became part of the Bishopric of Dorpat, on the Livonian border with Pskov and Novgorod.

vocontii.t: Confederation of the pre-Alps of the Drôme and Vaucluse that became an allied state of Rome, with its towns at Vaison and Die.
vocontii.o: The Vocontii held the mountains and valleys between the Rhône and the Alps, from the Drôme to Mont Ventoux. They were a league of smaller communities. Rome campaigned against them under Marcus Fulvius Flaccus in 124 BCE, during the first wars in Transalpine Gaul.
vocontii.r: After submission they kept unusual autonomy as a federated people, with two capitals, Vasio (Vaison-la-Romaine) and Lucus Augusti (Luc-en-Diois), later replaced by Dea Augusta (Die). The historian Pompeius Trogus came from a Vocontian family granted Roman citizenship.
vocontii.e: Their land was incorporated into Gallia Narbonensis. Vaison-la-Romaine preserves one of the largest excavated Roman towns in France, with houses, a theatre and a bridge still in use.

voluntii.t: People of north-east Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, often identified with the Ulaid who gave their name to Ulster.
voluntii.o: The Voluntii, or Uoluntii, appear in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 on the east coast of Ireland north of the Eblani, in the region of modern Counties Louth and Down. Their name is widely thought to be an early form of Ulaid, the people whose name survives in Ulster.
voluntii.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or institutions in classical sources. If the identification with the Ulaid is correct, they were the forerunners of the people whose heroic traditions, centred on Emain Macha, are preserved in the Ulster Cycle of Irish literature, though these tales were written down many centuries later.
voluntii.e: The Voluntii vanish from classical sources after Ptolemy. In early medieval Ireland the Ulaid formed the Kingdom of Ulaid, gradually pushed east of the River Bann by the Uí Néill.

vingulmark.t: Petty kingdom around the inner Oslofjord, a borderland between Norwegian and Danish power in the early Viking Age.
vingulmark.o: Vingulmark covered lands around the northern Oslofjord, roughly modern Østfold and the area around Oslo. It is known from the sagas as one of the small kingdoms that the kings of Vestfold sought to control in the 9th century.
vingulmark.r: The region was close to Denmark and was often under Danish influence, as was the whole area around the fjord called Viken. Its people farmed the fertile lowlands and traded by sea. No reliable details of its rulers or laws survive.
vingulmark.e: The sagas say Halfdan the Black won Vingulmark and that Harald Fairhair held it as part of his realm. Danish kings continued to claim Viken into the 11th century, but the district became part of the Kingdom of Norway.

viscounty-of-carcassonne.t: The Trencavel viscounties of Carcassonne, Béziers and Albi, the heart of Cathar country, destroyed by the Albigensian Crusade in 1209.
viscounty-of-carcassonne.o: In 1067 Raymond Bernard Trencavel, viscount of Albi and Nîmes, gained Carcassonne through his wife Ermengard, heiress of the counts of Carcassonne. Their son Bernard Ato IV built a principality across Carcassonne, Béziers, Albi and Razès, balancing between the counts of Toulouse and Barcelona.
viscounty-of-carcassonne.r: The Trencavels ruled from the walled city of Carcassonne, a centre of Occitan courtly culture. Their lands were the heartland of Catharism, and the viscounts tolerated the dissident church and its followers among the nobility. The Romanesque castle within Carcassonne's walls was their seat.
viscounty-of-carcassonne.e: In 1209 the Albigensian Crusade sacked Béziers and besieged Carcassonne. Raymond-Roger Trencavel surrendered and died in prison, and his lands went to Simon de Montfort. After a failed revolt in 1240 they were absorbed by the Kingdom of France.

venezuela.t: The South American republic that left Gran Colombia in 1830 and, transformed by the world's largest oil reserves, became the Bolivarian Republic under Hugo Chávez.
venezuela.o: In 1830 Venezuela, led by José Antonio Páez, seceded from Gran Colombia and adopted its own constitution, with Caracas as its capital. Páez dominated the early republic, which abolished slavery only in 1854.
venezuela.r: The Federal War of 1859 to 1863 gave the country a federal structure, and Antonio Guzmán Blanco modernised Caracas. Under the dictator Juan Vicente Gómez, from 1908 to 1935, oil was discovered, and Venezuela became a leading exporter. After the fall of Marcos Pérez Jiménez in 1958, the Punto Fijo pact created a two-party democracy. Venezuela co-founded OPEC in 1960 and nationalised its oil industry in 1976.
venezuela.e: Hugo Chávez, elected in 1998, introduced the 1999 constitution that renamed the state the Bolivarian Republic. Under Nicolás Maduro from 2013, economic collapse drove millions to emigrate. In January 2026 United States forces captured Maduro in Caracas.

viromandui.t: Belgic people of the upper Somme whose name lives on in the Vermandois and the town of Vermand.
viromandui.o: The Viromandui lived in the upper valleys of the Somme and Oise, between the Nervii, Ambiani and Suessiones. Caesar records that they promised ten thousand warriors to the Belgic league of 57 BCE.
viromandui.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions. Excavations at Vermand have revealed a large fortified site of the period.
viromandui.e: They fought beside the Nervii and Atrebates at the Battle of the Sabis in 57 BCE and were defeated. Under Rome their chief town became Augusta Viromanduorum (Saint-Quentin), and the medieval County of Vermandois kept their name.

voivodeship-of-serbia-and-banat-of-temes.t: Austrian crown land created after the 1848 revolution in southern Hungary, nominally Serbian but run by imperial officials from Temeschwar.
voivodeship-of-serbia-and-banat-of-temes.o: After the defeat of the Hungarian revolution, Emperor Franz Joseph rewarded the Serbs who had fought for the dynasty in the Serbian Vojvodina by creating, in November 1849, a separate crown land from Bačka, Banat and parts of Srem. He took the title of Grand Voivode himself and placed the government at Temeschwar.
voivodeship-of-serbia-and-banat-of-temes.r: The voivodeship was run by German-speaking officials under Vienna's neo-absolutist system, with a military governor and no elected assembly. Its borders were drawn to include large Romanian, German and Hungarian populations, so Serbs were only a minority, and Serb leaders were disappointed. Roads, railways and Danube trade developed, and Temeschwar grew as an industrial centre.
voivodeship-of-serbia-and-banat-of-temes.e: As Vienna sought compromise with Hungary, the crown land was abolished in 1860 and most of its territory returned to the Kingdom of Hungary (1526-1867), with parts of Srem going to Slavonia. The name survived in the modern Serbian province of Vojvodina.

virumaa.t: North-eastern Estonian county on the Gulf of Finland, conquered by Denmark around 1220 and long a frontier facing Novgorod.
virumaa.o: Virumaa, Vironia in Latin, stretched along Estonia's northern coast towards the Narva river. It was one of the largest ancient Estonian lands, with several parishes and hillforts; its main stronghold, Agelinde, is usually identified with Rakvere.
virumaa.r: Elders led the county's parishes, and its coast gave access to trade with Finland and Novgorod. Henry of Livonia records that Virumaa's elders submitted and accepted baptism under pressure from both the Germans and the Danes, who competed for the land.
virumaa.e: Virumaa passed under Danish rule after 1220, confirmed by the Treaty of Stensby in 1238, and formed part of the Duchy of Estonia (1219-1346). Novgorod attacked it repeatedly, notably at the Battle of Wesenberg in 1268. The region later belonged to the Livonian Order.

venda-kingdom.t: The kingdom of the Venda in the Soutpansberg mountains, known for its sacred Lake Fundudzi and its resistance to Boer expansion.
venda-kingdom.o: The Singo dynasty moved south across the Limpopo from the Zimbabwe plateau around 1700, according to tradition, and established its capital at Dzata in the Nzhelele valley. Its rulers brought stone-walling traditions and sacred drums, and they united the Venda of the Soutpansberg under one kingship.
venda-kingdom.r: The king was sacred and secluded, ruling through district chiefs and councillors. Thohoyandou, remembered as the greatest ruler, is said to have vanished mysteriously. Religion centred on ancestors and sacred sites such as Lake Fundudzi, and the domba initiation dance became famous. The Venda traded iron and copper goods, and in 1867 they forced Boer settlers to abandon Schoemansdal.
venda-kingdom.e: After Makhado's death in 1895, the South African Republic attacked his successor Mphephu in 1898; Mphephu fled across the Limpopo and Venda was annexed to the Transvaal. Venda later became a nominally independent apartheid homeland from 1979 to 1994.

vascones.t: The people of Navarre and ancestors of the Basques, whose lands held Pompey's foundation of Pompaelo, modern Pamplona.
vascones.o: The Vascones lived in the upper Ebro valley and western Pyrenees, roughly modern Navarre and parts of Aragon and La Rioja, by the 3rd century BCE. They probably spoke an early form of Basque, related to Aquitanian across the mountains.
vascones.r: They lived in hill towns and villages, farming the Ebro plain and herding in the mountains. Their towns included Calagurris and later Pompaelo, and they minted coins with Iberian-script legends. They had no single ruler and were organised in local communities.
vascones.e: In the winter of 75 to 74 BCE Pompey camped in their territory, giving his name to Pompaelo. Calagurris backed Sertorius and fell in 72 BCE after a famous siege. The Vascones were absorbed into Hispania Citerior, but their language survived and later the Kingdom of Navarre arose in their land.

viceroyalty-of-kush.t: Egypt's colonial administration of Nubia in the New Kingdom, governed by the 'King's Son of Kush' and rich in gold.
viceroyalty-of-kush.o: After Thutmose I destroyed Kerma around 1500 BCE, the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom annexed Nubia as far as the Fourth Cataract. It was governed by a viceroy with the title 'King's Son of Kush', divided into Wawat (Lower Nubia), administered from Aniba, and Kush (Upper Nubia).
viceroyalty-of-kush.r: The viceroys collected tribute in gold, ivory, ebony, cattle and soldiers, and Nubian gold mines in the Wadi Allaqi made Egypt the richest power of its age. Pharaohs built temple towns at Soleb, Sesebi, Gebel Barkal and Abu Simbel. Nubian elites were educated at the Egyptian court, and Egyptian religion, especially the cult of Amun, took deep root. Known viceroys include Merymose and Huy.
viceroyalty-of-kush.e: Around 1080 BCE the viceroy Panehesy fought the High Priest of Amun in Thebes and withdrew to Nubia, which then slipped from Egyptian control. Egyptian religion and kingship persisted locally and later inspired the Kushite Empire of Napata.

volcae-tectosages.t: Celtic people of Toulouse, kin of the Galatians of Anatolia, whose sacred gold was seized by a Roman consul in 106 BCE.
volcae-tectosages.o: The Volcae were a Celtic people who settled in Languedoc in the 3rd century BCE. The Tectosages held the western part around Tolosa (Toulouse) on the Garonne. Other bands of the same name joined the migrations into the Balkans and Anatolia, where the Galatian Tectosages settled around Ancyra.
volcae-tectosages.r: Tolosa controlled the corridor between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Strabo describes a rich sanctuary where gold and silver were sunk in sacred lakes. They became allies of Rome after the conquest of the Province in 121 BCE.
volcae-tectosages.e: In 107 BCE they rebelled with the help of the migrating Cimbri and Tigurini. The consul Quintus Servilius Caepio retook Tolosa in 106 BCE and seized its treasure, the gold of Tolosa, which vanished on the way to Rome. Their land became part of Gallia Narbonensis.

vestfold.t: Viking Age kingdom on the west shore of the Oslofjord, home of the Oseberg and Gokstad ship burials and of the dynasty that unified Norway.
vestfold.o: Vestfold's rich farmland and harbours made it a centre of power by the 8th century. The Borre mounds hold one of Scandinavia's largest royal cemeteries, and Frankish annals of 813 record Danish kings campaigning in Vestfold to assert their overlordship, showing it lay in the Danish sphere.
vestfold.r: The kings controlled Kaupang, the trading town the traveller Ohthere called Sciringes heal, where goods from the Frankish, Danish and Arab worlds were exchanged. Royal display reached its height in the Oseberg ship burial of 834 and the Gokstad burial around 900. Snorri's Ynglinga saga traces the kings back to the Swedish Ynglings.
vestfold.e: According to the sagas, Halfdan the Black extended Vestfold's power over the Upplands, and his son Harald Fairhair conquered western Norway, traditionally at Hafrsfjord around 872. Vestfold thus became the cradle of the Kingdom of Norway, and its ship burials are among the best-known finds of the Viking Age.

venetian-negroponte.t: Venetian-ruled Euboea, a key Aegean naval base whose fall to Mehmed II in 1470 was one of the great blows to Venice's empire.
venetian-negroponte.o: Venice had long dominated the Triarchy of Negroponte through its bailo in the town of Negroponte (Chalcis). As the Lombard triarchs weakened in the face of the Turks and the Catalans, Venice took over their lands, and by 1390 ruled the whole island directly.
venetian-negroponte.r: A Venetian bailo and councillors governed from the fortified town on the Euripus strait, where a bridge linked the island to the mainland. Negroponte was a major port of call for Venetian galleys, a grain and silk market and a base for watching the Aegean. A Greek Orthodox majority lived under a Latin elite.
venetian-negroponte.e: In 1470 Mehmed II besieged Negroponte by land and sea and stormed it in July; the bailo Paolo Erizzo was killed. The loss shocked Venice and left Euboea Ottoman until the Greek War of Independence.

vyatichi.t: The easternmost East Slavic tribe, settled on the upper Oka, and the last to give up its independence and its pagan gods.
vyatichi.o: The Primary Chronicle says the Vyatichi descended from Vyatko, a leader who came from the west, and settled on the upper and middle Oka. Archaeology dates Slavic settlement there to the 8th century, where newcomers mingled with Baltic and Finnic inhabitants. Like their southern neighbours they paid tribute to the Khazars.
vyatichi.r: Hidden in dense forest far from the Dnieper, they lived in small fortified settlements under their own chiefs and kept their clan customs. They traded furs, honey and wax along the Oka and Volga, and hoards of Arab silver dirhams are common in their lands. They clung to pagan burial rites well into the 12th century, and the missionary Kuksha was killed among them.
vyatichi.e: Sviatoslav I forced them to pay tribute to Kiev in the 960s, Vladimir I subdued them again in 981 and 982, and Vladimir Monomakh campaigned against their chief Khodota around 1100. Their lands were divided between the principalities of Chernigov, Ryazan and Rostov-Suzdal, and later formed the heart of the Grand Duchy of Moscow.

varduli.t: A people of the western Pyrenean coast in Gipuzkoa and Álava, among the ancestors of the Basques.
varduli.o: The Varduli lived in the area of modern Gipuzkoa and parts of Álava and Navarre in the later Iron Age, between the Caristii and the Vascones. Whether they spoke an early form of Basque or a Celtic language is debated.
varduli.r: Little is known of their society. They lived from herding, farming, fishing and the iron of their hills, and Ptolemy names towns such as Gebala and Menosca. Strabo includes them among the rough mountain peoples of the north.
varduli.e: They came under Roman rule as part of the conquest of the north completed in the Cantabrian Wars of 19 BCE, and later supplied auxiliary troops, including a cohort of Varduli that served in Britain. Their land became part of Hispania Tarraconensis.

venetian-cyprus.t: Cyprus under the Republic of Venice from 1489 to 1571, a heavily fortified frontier colony lost to the Ottomans in a famous siege of Famagusta.
venetian-cyprus.o: Venetian influence in the Kingdom of Cyprus grew through the marriage of King James II to the Venetian Catherine Cornaro. After his death and that of their infant son, Venice controlled Catherine's government, and in 1489 forced her to abdicate and cede the island to the Republic.
venetian-cyprus.r: A Venetian lieutenant and councillors ruled from Nicosia, keeping the old Frankish nobility while taxing heavily. Cyprus exported cotton, sugar, salt and wine, and paid tribute to Mamluk Egypt and later the Ottomans. Fearing invasion, Venice rebuilt the walls of Famagusta and in 1567 built new star-shaped bastions around Nicosia.
venetian-cyprus.e: The Ottomans invaded in 1570. Nicosia fell in September 1570, and Famagusta surrendered in August 1571 after a long siege; its commander Marco Antonio Bragadin was flayed alive. Cyprus became an Ottoman province.

vyatka-land.t: A remote self-governing land of Russian settlers on the Vyatka river, famous for river pirates and finally conquered by Moscow in 1489.
vyatka-land.o: Settlers from Novgorod and other Russian lands moved into the Vyatka basin among the Udmurt and Mari peoples. A late local tale dates their arrival to 1181, but this is traditional and uncertain. Their main town, Khlynov, later Kirov, is first reliably mentioned in the 14th century.
vyatka-land.r: Vyatka had no princely dynasty for most of its history and was run by assemblies and elected leaders, much like the Novgorod Republic. Its people farmed, trapped furs and joined the ushkuiniki, river raiders who attacked towns along the Volga and Kama. It was at times subject to the princes of Nizhny Novgorod and Moscow and allied with the Kazan Tatars.
vyatka-land.e: Ivan III sent a large army against Vyatka in 1489. Khlynov surrendered, its leading men were executed or deported, and the land was annexed to the Grand Duchy of Moscow. Its later history is that of an ordinary Russian province.

vediantii.t: Ligurian people of the hills behind Nice whose town Cemenelum became the capital of the Roman Maritime Alps.
vediantii.o: Known from Pliny and Ptolemy, the Vediantii lived in the hills of the lower Var and Paillon valleys, behind the Greek port of Nikaia (Nice), a colony of Massalia.
vediantii.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. Like other Alpine Ligurians they lived in hill forts and practised herding and farming.
vediantii.e: They were brought under Roman control in the Alpine campaigns of Augustus, and in 14 BCE their land became part of the province of Alpes Maritimae. Their settlement of Cemenelum (Cimiez, now part of Nice) became its capital, with an amphitheatre and baths that still survive.

venetian-tinos.t: Venetian-ruled island of Tinos, the last Venetian possession in the Aegean, which held out until 1715 and kept a lasting Catholic community.
venetian-tinos.o: In 1390 the last of the Ghisi family, Giorgio III, died and left the Lordship of Tinos and Mykonos to Venice. The Republic took over the two islands, first through lessees and later through officials sent from Venice, making Tinos part of its overseas Stato da Mar.
venetian-tinos.r: A Venetian rettore governed from the hilltop fortress of Exobourgo, which protected the islanders from pirates and Turkish raids. Tinos produced silk, wine and other goods, and a significant part of its population became Catholic, alongside an Orthodox majority. Mykonos was lost to the Ottomans in 1537, but Tinos repelled several attacks.
venetian-tinos.e: At the start of the Ottoman-Venetian war of 1714-1718, a large Ottoman fleet attacked Tinos in 1715 and its governor surrendered. The Treaty of Passarowitz confirmed Ottoman rule. Tinos still has a substantial Catholic community.

volga-bulgaria.t: A Muslim Bulgar state on the middle Volga that grew rich on the fur trade and was the northernmost outpost of Islam for three centuries.
volga-bulgaria.o: Bulgar tribes who left Old Great Bulgaria after the Khazar conquest moved north to the confluence of the Volga and Kama during the 7th and 8th centuries, ruling over Finnic and other local peoples. They remained tributaries of the Khazars until the 10th century, when the Khazar state weakened.
volga-bulgaria.r: In 922 the ruler Almish received an embassy from the Abbasid caliph, described by Ibn Fadlan, and adopted Islam. Bolghar and later Bilyar were large trading cities where furs, honey, wax and slaves from the north were exchanged for Islamic silver and goods. The emirs minted coins and fought frequent wars with Kievan Rus' and Vladimir-Suzdal.
volga-bulgaria.e: The Bulgars defeated a Mongol force at the Samara Bend in 1223, but in 1236 the Mongols returned, destroyed Bilyar and conquered the country. It became part of the Golden Horde, with Bolghar briefly serving as a Horde capital. Both the Volga Tatars and the Chuvash claim the Bulgars among their ancestors.

viscounty-of-turenne.t: A self-governing viscounty in the Limousin and Quercy that kept its own estates and tax privileges until it was sold to the French crown in 1738.
viscounty-of-turenne.o: Viscounts of Turenne appear in the late 10th century, based at a castle on a hill near Brive in the Limousin. Their lands stretched into Quercy, and the family survived among the competing lords of Aquitaine by playing English and French kings against each other.
viscounty-of-turenne.r: The viscounts enjoyed unusual privileges: the right to summon their own estates, to raise taxes and, by tradition, to mint coin, with near exemption from royal taxation. In 1444 the viscounty passed to the La Tour d'Auvergne family. Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, a Huguenot leader, married into the house of La Marck and became prince of Sedan.
viscounty-of-turenne.e: In 1738, burdened by debts, Charles-Godefroy de La Tour d'Auvergne sold the viscounty to Louis XV, and it was absorbed into the Kingdom of France. Its privileges ended, and the region lost its tax exemptions.
ru: Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Duke of Bouillon

vatican-city.t: The world's smallest sovereign state, an enclave in Rome created in 1929 to guarantee the independence of the pope and the Holy See.
vatican-city.o: After Italy took Rome from the Papal States in 1870, the popes refused to recognise the loss and considered themselves prisoners in the Vatican. The Roman Question was settled by the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, signed by Cardinal Pietro Gasparri for Pope Pius XI and Benito Mussolini for the Kingdom of Italy, creating Vatican City.
vatican-city.r: The state covers about 44 hectares around Saint Peter's Basilica and the Apostolic Palace. The pope is an absolute elective monarch, elected by cardinals in conclave, and governs through a commission and a governor; the Swiss Guard protects him. Vatican City supports the worldwide government of the Holy See, with Vatican Radio founded in 1931, the Vatican Museums and the Apostolic Library.
vatican-city.e: The Second Vatican Council of 1962–1965 transformed the Church's relations with the modern world. The concordat with Italy was revised in 1984. Vatican City continues today; Pope Leo XIV was elected in 2025.

vacomagi.t: People of north-east Scotland around Moray and Strathspey, to whom Ptolemy assigned four towns, among them Pinnata Castra and Tuesis.
vacomagi.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Vacomagi in the northern Highlands and lowlands, usually located in Moray, Strathspey and parts of Banffshire. He lists four settlements in their land, Bannatia, Tamia, Pinnata Castra and Tuesis, more than for most northern peoples, suggesting a well-populated territory.
vacomagi.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. The fertile Laich of Moray supported farming communities, and the great promontory fort at Burghead, later a major Pictish centre, has sometimes been identified with Pinnata Castra, though this is uncertain. Roman marching camps reach into the region, showing the passage of Roman armies in the late 1st and early 3rd centuries.
vacomagi.e: The Vacomagi do not appear after Ptolemy. Their lands later formed a heartland of the northern Picts, part of the Kingdom of Fortriu and the wider Kingdom of the Picts.

veliocasses.t: Belgic people of the lower Seine whose town Rotomagus became Rouen.
veliocasses.o: The Veliocasses held the Vexin and the lower Seine valley. Caesar reports that they promised warriors to the Belgic league of 57 BCE together with the Viromandui.
veliocasses.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Their position on the Seine gave them a share of river trade to the Channel.
veliocasses.e: They submitted in 57 BCE and later sent men to relieve Alesia. Under Rome their chief town Rotomagus grew into an important river port, the origin of Rouen, later capital of the Duchy of Normandy. Their name survives in the Vexin.

varmland.t: Forested petty kingdom north of Lake Vänern, known mostly from the Norse sagas, later absorbed into the Swedish realm.
varmland.o: Värmland, the land around the rivers flowing into Lake Vänern, is known mainly from Icelandic sagas written centuries later. Snorri Sturluson's Ynglinga saga tells that Olof the Tree-Feller, driven from Uppsala, cleared the forests here and founded a new line of kings.
varmland.r: Its people lived by farming, iron extraction from bog ore and forest trades, and met at their own assemblies. The sagas describe Värmland as a borderland contested by Norwegian, Svear and Geatish kings, with local kings or jarls of uncertain historical reality.
varmland.e: By around 1000 Värmland was drawn into the orbit of the Swedish kings, although Norwegian rulers such as Olaf Haraldsson also tried to claim it. It became a province of the Kingdom of Sweden, keeping its own law and lawman in the Middle Ages.

volaterrae.t: Northern Etruscan city on a lofty hill, master of a large territory and famous for its alabaster urns, which later withstood Sulla for two years.
volaterrae.o: Volaterrae, Etruscan Velathri, modern Volterra, occupies a high ridge between the Cecina and Era valleys. Settled from the Villanovan period, it became one of the largest Etruscan cities by the 4th century BCE, when walls more than 7 km long enclosed the town and its fields. Its territory reached the sea and included mines and salt springs.
volaterrae.r: Volaterrae prospered from farming, salt, copper and timber. In the Hellenistic period its workshops produced hundreds of carved alabaster and tufa cinerary urns showing mythological scenes and portraits of the dead, now in the Guarnacci Museum. The Porta all'Arco, an arched city gate with sculpted heads, survives. Local families such as the Caecinae remained prominent well into Roman times.
volaterrae.e: Volaterrae became a Roman ally in the 3rd century BCE and supplied grain and timber for Scipio's fleet in 205 BCE. Having backed Marius, it held out against Sulla's siege from 82 to 79 BCE, and later became a municipium. The satirist Persius was born there, and Volterra keeps its alabaster craft.

viducasses.t: Small Gallic people of the Caen plain whose Roman town at Vieux has yielded the famous Thorigny marble.
viducasses.o: Known from Pliny and Ptolemy, the Viducasses lived south of modern Caen in lower Normandy. They were probably included among the Armorican peoples in Caesar's time.
viducasses.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. Their chief town, Aregenua, lay at Vieux.
viducasses.e: Under Rome Aregenua became a prosperous civitas capital with baths and fine houses. The Thorigny marble, an inscription of 238 CE, honours one of its citizens, Titus Sennius Sollemnis. The civitas later merged with that of the Baiocasses.

viceroyalty-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.t: The last viceroyalty created by Spain in the Americas, ruled from Buenos Aires, whose crisis in 1810 began Argentina's independence.
viceroyalty-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.o: To counter Portuguese expansion and smuggling, Charles III created the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776, with Buenos Aires as its capital and Pedro de Cevallos as first viceroy. It joined the governorates of Buenos Aires, Paraguay and Tucumán with Cuyo and the Royal Audiencia of Charcas, including the silver of Potosí.
viceroyalty-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.r: Silver from Potosí now flowed out through Buenos Aires, which boomed after the free-trade regulation of 1778 opened it to direct trade with Spain. Intendancies replaced the old governorates in 1782. Hides and salted meat were growing exports. In 1806 and 1807 British forces invaded Buenos Aires and Montevideo, and local militias under Santiago de Liniers drove them out, boosting Creole confidence.
viceroyalty-of-the-rio-de-la-plata.e: After Napoleon's capture of the Spanish king, the May Revolution of 1810 deposed the viceroy and created the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata. Paraguay and Upper Peru broke away, and royalist Montevideo fell in 1814.

visby.t: Walled Hanseatic town on Gotland, one of the great trading centres of the medieval Baltic, whose walls and churches still stand.
visby.o: Visby grew on Gotland's west coast as a harbour of the Gotland farmers' republic. In 1161 Henry the Lion of Saxony confirmed the rights of German merchants trading on Gotland, and German traders settled alongside Gotlanders, making Visby the base of the Community of Gotland Merchants who traded with Novgorod.
visby.r: The town was run by a council of German and Gotlandic merchants and acted with growing independence from the rural island. Around 1300 it built a 3.4-kilometre stone wall, and it filled with stone warehouses and more than a dozen churches. Its maritime law influenced other Baltic ports, and it was a leading member of the early Hanseatic League.
visby.e: Conflict with the rural Gotlanders led to civil war in 1288. In 1361 Valdemar IV of Denmark took Visby after defeating the farmers outside its walls, and the town surrendered. Its importance declined as Lübeck rose. Visby is now a World Heritage Site.

viscounty-of-limoges.t: A viscounty in the Limousin that outlasted most feudal lordships and passed by inheritance to Brittany, Albret and finally the future Henry IV.
viscounty-of-limoges.o: Viscounts appear at Limoges in the late 9th century as deputies of the counts of Poitou, who as dukes of Aquitaine claimed overlordship of the Limousin. The office became hereditary in a local family, which governed the city's castle quarter while the bishop and the abbey of Saint-Martial dominated the rest of the town.
viscounty-of-limoges.r: The viscounts were middling lords caught between Aquitaine, the Plantagenet kings and the French crown, often clashing with their own townsmen and with English overlords; Richard the Lionheart died in 1199 besieging Châlus, a castle in the viscounty. Limoges itself was known for its enamel work and as a pilgrimage centre on the road to Compostela.
viscounty-of-limoges.e: Through marriage the viscounty passed to the dukes of Brittany in 1275, then to the Blois-Penthièvre line and the house of Albret. It reached the Bourbons through Jeanne d'Albret, and when her son Henry IV became king in 1589 it was merged with the crown.

voivodeship-of-seneslau.t: Romanian voivodeship east of the Olt, one of the earliest Romanian polities recorded, known from a Hungarian royal charter of 1247.
voivodeship-of-seneslau.o: The only clear source is the charter of 1247 by which Béla IV of Hungary granted lands to the Knights Hospitaller. It mentions the land of Seneslau, voivode of the Romanians (Olati), east of the Olt in what became Wallachia, which was left in Romanian hands.
voivodeship-of-seneslau.r: Nothing is known of its government beyond the charter, which treats Seneslau as a tributary of the Hungarian crown, obliged to share revenues and provide military aid. His power probably rested on local knezes and the routes between the Carpathians and the Danube.
voivodeship-of-seneslau.e: It is not mentioned again, and its fate is unknown. Historians see it as one of the polities later united in the Principality of Wallachia by Basarab I.

vladimir-suzdal.t: The grand principality of north-eastern Rus', centre of white-stone architecture and the political root of Muscovite Russia.
vladimir-suzdal.o: In 1157 Andrei Bogolyubsky, son of Yuri Dolgoruky, moved the capital of the Principality of Rostov-Suzdal to Vladimir on the Klyazma. He built the Golden Gate, the Dormition Cathedral and the Church of the Intercession on the Nerl, and in 1169 his army sacked Kiev, though he stayed in the north.
vladimir-suzdal.r: Andrei was murdered by his boyars in 1174, and his brother Vsevolod the Big Nest ruled from 1176 to 1212, dominating north-eastern Rus' and fathering many princes. After the Mongols sacked Vladimir in 1238 and killed Yuri II on the Sit river, the grand-princely title was granted by the khans of the Golden Horde through a patent, the yarlyk, while the land split into appanages.
vladimir-suzdal.e: Alexander Nevsky held the title from 1252, and his descendants in Moscow and the princes of Tver fought for it. In 1331 Ivan I Kalita of the Grand Duchy of Moscow became sole grand prince, and Vladimir's title was merged into Moscow's.

votadini.t: People of south-east Scotland and Northumberland centred on Traprain Law, who lived beside Roman Britain and became the post-Roman Gododdin.
votadini.o: Ptolemy places the Votadini on the east coast between the Firth of Forth and the Tyne in the 2nd century. They descended from Iron Age communities of Lothian and the Borders, and their great hillfort at Traprain Law in East Lothian was a major centre from before the Roman arrival in the 80s.
votadini.r: Unlike neighbours such as the Selgovae, the Votadini show few signs of hostility to Rome, and many historians think they were a friendly buffer people beyond Hadrian's Wall. Roman goods reached Traprain Law in quantity, culminating in the Traprain Law Treasure, a hoard of cut Roman silver buried in the early 5th century, perhaps a payment or subsidy. Their economy rested on mixed farming.
votadini.e: After Roman rule ended, the Votadini developed into the Kingdom of Gododdin, centred on Din Eidyn, Edinburgh, whose warriors are celebrated in the Welsh poem Y Gododdin. Their name in its Welsh form, Guotodin, carried the people into the early medieval period.

venetian-ionian-islands.t: Venice's possessions in the Ionian Sea, centred on Corfu, which stayed outside Ottoman rule and took on a lasting Italian character.
venetian-ionian-islands.o: In 1386 Corfu, previously under the Angevins of Naples, placed itself under Venetian protection; Venice formally bought the rights in 1402. It later added Zakynthos (1485), Cephalonia (1500), Ithaca, Kythira and finally Lefkada (1684), gaining control over the sea route between the Adriatic and the eastern Mediterranean.
venetian-ionian-islands.r: A Venetian provveditore generale in Corfu governed with local councils of island nobles registered in a Golden Book. Italian became the language of administration and the elite, while the majority stayed Greek Orthodox. Olive oil and currants were the main exports. Corfu's fortresses withstood Ottoman sieges in 1537 and 1716, the latter under Johann Matthias von der Schulenburg.
venetian-ionian-islands.e: When Napoleon ended the Venetian Republic in 1797, the Treaty of Campo Formio gave the islands to France, creating the French Ionian Islands. Their distinct Italian-Greek culture survived into the Septinsular Republic and British rule.

visigothic-kingdom.t: Gothic kingdom first at Toulouse, then at Toledo, that ruled Iberia for two centuries until the Muslim conquest of 711.
visigothic-kingdom.o: After sacking Rome in 410 under Alaric, the Visigoths moved into Gaul and Spain. In 418 Rome settled them as federates in Aquitaine, with Toulouse as their capital, under King Wallia. Theodoric I died fighting Attila on the Catalaunian Plains in 451, and Euric made the kingdom fully independent and expanded deep into Hispania.
visigothic-kingdom.r: Gothic warriors ruled a mostly Roman population, at first under separate laws. The kings were Arian until Reccared converted to Catholicism in 589, after which the Councils of Toledo became central to government. Leovigild conquered the Kingdom of the Suebi, and Recceswinth issued the Visigothic Code in 654.
visigothic-kingdom.e: Clovis defeated Alaric II at Vouillé in 507, and the capital moved to Toledo. In 711 Tariq ibn Ziyad defeated King Roderic, and the Umayyad Caliphate conquered Iberia; the last Visigothic outpost in Septimania fell around 720. The Christian kingdoms of the north claimed Visigothic descent.

vichy-france.t: The authoritarian French State of Marshal Pétain, which collaborated with Nazi Germany and helped deport Jews from France.
vichy-france.o: After the German victory in 1940 and the armistice of 22 June, France was divided into an occupied north and an unoccupied south. On 10 July the parliament meeting at Vichy voted full powers to Marshal Philippe Pétain, ending the French Third Republic and creating the French State.
vichy-france.r: Pétain led a 'National Revolution' under the motto Work, Family, Fatherland, abolishing parliament and promoting conservative Catholic values. Vichy chose collaboration after Pétain met Hitler at Montoire in 1940. Its own anti-Jewish laws and its police's role in round-ups, such as the Vel d'Hiv in 1942, contributed to the deportation of about 76,000 Jews from France.
vichy-france.e: Germany occupied the south in November 1942, leaving Vichy little power. After the Allied landings of 1944 the regime collapsed; its leaders were taken to Sigmaringen in Germany. Pétain was sentenced to death, commuted to life imprisonment, and Pierre Laval was executed.

velabri.t: People of south-west Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, usually placed on the Atlantic coast of Kerry beside the Iverni.
velabri.o: The Velabri are known only from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which places them on the south-west coast of Ireland, south of the Gangani (Ireland) and west of the Iverni, roughly in modern County Kerry. Ptolemy's information on Ireland came from earlier reports by sailors along the Atlantic coast.
velabri.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or customs. The peninsulas of Kerry were a land of stone forts, promontory forts and pastoral farming, and the region later produced many ogham stones, showing that Irish-speaking communities with strong lineage traditions lived there by the 5th century.
velabri.e: The Velabri do not appear in any later source, and no Irish population name has been securely matched with theirs. Their region later formed part of the Kingdom of Munster and the lands of peoples such as the Corcu Duibne and the Ciarraige Luachra.

vestini.t: Sabellic people of the Gran Sasso and the Aterno valley in Abruzzo, whose territory produced the famous Warrior of Capestrano statue.
vestini.o: The Vestini lived in the high valleys around the Gran Sasso and the middle Aterno, reaching the Adriatic coast near Pinna (Penne). Ancient writers counted them among the Sabellian peoples; their culture developed locally from the early 1st millennium BCE.
vestini.r: They lived in scattered villages, hill forts and towns such as Pinna, Aveia and Peltuinum, keeping flocks that moved between mountain and lowland pastures. The Warrior of Capestrano, a life-size limestone statue of the 6th century BCE with a South Picene inscription, was found in a Vestine cemetery and is the most famous work of Italic sculpture. Their political organisation is otherwise poorly known.
vestini.e: Allied with the Samnites, the Vestini were defeated by Rome in 325 BCE and made an alliance around 302 BCE. They joined the Italian revolt in the Social War and were defeated in 89 BCE, then received citizenship and were absorbed into Roman Italy.

voivodeship-of-transylvania.t: Eastern province of medieval Hungary ruled by royal voivodes, home to Hungarian nobles, Saxons and Székelys, which became an autonomous principality in 1570.
voivodeship-of-transylvania.o: After Stephen I annexed the Realm of the Gyulas in 1003, Transylvania was organised in royal counties. From 1176, when Leustach is named voivode, a royal official with that Slavic title governed the province for the kings of Hungary.
voivodeship-of-transylvania.r: The voivode headed the counties of the nobility, while German settlers (Saxons) had their own rights under the Andreanum of 1224 and the Székelys formed a separate military community. Romanians formed much of the peasantry. Voivodes such as Ladislaus Kán around 1300 acted almost as independent rulers. After a peasant revolt in 1437, nobles, Saxons and Székelys formed the Union of Three Nations, which excluded Romanians. John Hunyadi served as voivode from 1441.
voivodeship-of-transylvania.e: After Mohács in 1526, voivode John Zápolya became king of eastern Hungary. His son John Sigismund renounced the royal title by the Treaty of Speyer in 1570, and the land became the Principality of Transylvania under Ottoman overlordship.

venicones.t: People of Fife and the Tay region recorded by Ptolemy, whose lands later formed a core region of the Picts.
venicones.o: The Venicones appear in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, generally placed in Fife and perhaps Kinross and southern Angus, between the Forth and the Tay, with a settlement called Orrea. They descended from local Iron Age communities living in hillforts, crannogs and open farmsteads on fertile lowland soils.
venicones.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or institutions. Their territory lay close to the Roman frontier: forts along the Gask Ridge and the legionary base at Carpow on the Tay, built under Severus around 208, show heavy Roman activity. Some historians think they are the people later called Maeatae, or part of them.
venicones.e: The Venicones disappear from the written record after Ptolemy. Their lands later formed the Pictish province of Fib, which gave its name to Fife, within the Kingdom of the Picts.

viceroyalty-of-new-granada.t: The Spanish viceroyalty of northern South America, ruled from Bogotá, whose collapse in the wars of independence gave rise to Gran Colombia.
viceroyalty-of-new-granada.o: Spain created the Viceroyalty of New Granada in 1717 out of the New Kingdom of Granada and other territories of the Viceroyalty of Peru, to defend the Caribbean coast and improve administration. Abolished in 1723 for lack of revenue, it was permanently restored in 1739, covering modern Colombia, Ecuador, Panama and Venezuela.
viceroyalty-of-new-granada.r: The viceroy ruled from Santa Fe de Bogotá. Cartagena's fortifications withstood the British attack under Edward Vernon in 1741, led by Blas de Lezo and Viceroy Sebastián de Eslava. Gold from the Chocó and Antioquia was the main export. In 1777 Venezuela was separated as a captaincy general. The Comunero revolt of 1781 opposed new taxes. The Royal Botanical Expedition of José Celestino Mutis from 1783 trained a generation of Creole scientists.
viceroyalty-of-new-granada.e: A junta in Bogotá on 20 July 1810 began the movement for independence. Pablo Morillo reconquered the territory in 1816, but Simón Bolívar's victory at Boyacá in 1819 ended Spanish rule and led to the creation of Gran Colombia.

viceroyalty-of-peru.t: Spain's great South American viceroyalty, ruled from Lima, whose silver from Potosí flowed across the world for nearly three centuries.
viceroyalty-of-peru.o: Charles V created the Viceroyalty of Peru through the New Laws of 1542, replacing the governorates of New Castile and New Toledo. The first viceroy, Blasco Núñez Vela, was killed by rebels under Gonzalo Pizarro in 1546, and royal authority was only restored when Pedro de la Gasca defeated Pizarro in 1548.
viceroyalty-of-peru.r: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo, from 1569 to 1581, reorganised the colony: indigenous people were moved into reducciones, and the mita drafted labour for the silver mines of Potosí and the mercury mines of Huancavelica. Lima, the City of the Kings, was home to the Audiencia, the University of San Marcos, founded in 1551, and the Inquisition. Its territory at first covered nearly all of Spanish South America.
viceroyalty-of-peru.e: The Bourbon reforms removed New Granada in 1717 and Río de la Plata in 1776. After the revolt of Túpac Amaru II in 1780 was crushed, Peru remained a royalist stronghold until San Martín proclaimed independence in 1821 and the Battle of Ayacucho in 1824 ended Spanish rule.

veneti.t: Seafaring Gallic people of southern Brittany who controlled Atlantic trade with Britain until Caesar destroyed their fleet in 56 BCE.
veneti.o: The Veneti held the coast of the Morbihan, a landscape of tidal inlets and promontories, with Darioritum (Vannes) as their later chief town. They dominated the sea routes between Armorica and Britain and were the strongest of the Armorican peoples.
veneti.r: Caesar describes their tall oak ships with flat bottoms, iron bolts and leather sails, built to ride Atlantic storms, and their towns set on headlands cut off by the tide. They levied tolls on other seafarers and grew rich on trade in tin and goods with Britain.
veneti.e: In 56 BCE they detained Roman officers sent for grain, and Caesar built a fleet on the Loire. Decimus Brutus defeated them in a calm, probably in Quiberon Bay, by cutting their rigging with hooked poles. Caesar executed their council and sold the people into slavery; Vannes keeps their name.

vetulonia.t: Early Etruscan power in the metal-rich hills of northern Etruria, which Roman tradition credited as the source of the fasces and other symbols of office.
vetulonia.o: Vetulonia, Etruscan Vatluna, grew on a hill overlooking the former Lake Prile, then a lagoon open to the sea, in the 9th and 8th centuries BCE. Its wealth came from the copper, iron and silver of the nearby Colline Metallifere, and it was one of the leading Etruscan centres of the 8th and 7th centuries BCE.
vetulonia.r: Rich 'circle tombs' and great tumuli such as the Pietrera reveal an aristocracy enriched by metals and trade with Sardinia and the eastern Mediterranean. Its goldsmiths excelled in granulation. The 'Tomb of the Lictor' contained an iron double axe with rods, and the Roman poet Silius Italicus wrote that Rome borrowed the fasces, curule chair and purple-bordered toga from Vetulonia.
vetulonia.e: Vetulonia declined from the 6th century BCE as Populonia and Rusellae grew. It revived in the Hellenistic period, minting coins, and passed under Roman control in the early 3rd century BCE, later becoming a municipium. Its exact location was only confirmed in the 19th century; the village of Colonna di Buriano took the ancient name in 1887.

viceroyalty-of-carchemish.t: The Hittite viceroyalty of Carchemish, which governed Syria for the Hittite kings and outlived the empire's fall.
viceroyalty-of-carchemish.o: Suppiluliuma I of the Hittite Empire took Carchemish, a great Euphrates crossing city, after a siege c. 1327 BCE, ending the Mitanni Empire's hold on Syria. He made his son Piyassili, known by the Hurrian name Sharri-Kushuh, king of Carchemish.
viceroyalty-of-carchemish.r: The kings of Carchemish acted as viceroys for the Hittite great king, supervising Syrian vassals such as Ugarit, Emar and Amurru, settling their disputes and collecting tribute. They belonged to the Hittite royal family and kept a court with Hurrian and Luwian traditions.
viceroyalty-of-carchemish.e: When Hattusa fell around 1180 BCE, Carchemish survived. Kuzi-Teshub took the title great king, and his heirs founded the Neo-Hittite Kingdom of Carchemish and kingdoms such as Melid, carrying Hittite traditions into the Iron Age.

vistulans.t: A West Slavic tribe of the upper Vistula, centred on Krakow, whose pagan prince was warned by Saint Methodius to accept baptism.
vistulans.o: The Vistulans settled the upper Vistula basin in what is now southern Poland, with their centre on Wawel Hill in Krakow and another stronghold at Wislica. They are named in the 9th-century list known as the Bavarian Geographer and in the Life of Saint Methodius.
vistulans.r: Their territory was a fertile, densely settled region on trade routes between Bohemia, Moravia and Rus', and the rich hill fort at Wawel suggests a wealthy ruling elite. The Life of Methodius tells of a powerful pagan prince on the Vistula who persecuted Christians and was urged to be baptised willingly before he was baptised by force in a foreign land.
vistulans.e: The prophecy seems to have come true when Svatopluk of Great Moravia brought the Vistulans under his rule around 880. After Moravia collapsed, the region passed to the Duchy of Bohemia, and around 990 the Duchy of Poland took Krakow, which later became the Polish royal capital.

vettones.t: A Celtic-speaking people of the western Meseta, known for their great hillforts and the stone boars and bulls called verracos.
vettones.o: The Vettones emerged in the second half of the first millennium BCE between the Douro and Tagus rivers, in modern Ávila, Salamanca and Cáceres and parts of Portugal. They grew out of the Iron Age Cogotas culture and were related to their Lusitanian and Celtiberian neighbours.
vettones.r: They lived in large fortified hillforts such as Las Cogotas, Ulaca and El Raso, and their economy was dominated by cattle and pig herding. Hundreds of granite sculptures of boars and bulls, the verracos, mark their territory and probably protected herds or pastures. Their society had warrior elites, and they spoke a Celtic or para-Celtic language.
vettones.e: Often allied with the Lusitanians, they resisted Rome through the 2nd century BCE and were finally subdued after campaigns including Julius Caesar's of 61 BCE. Their lands became part of the province of Lusitania, with towns such as Salmantica and Augustobriga.

vellavi.t: Gallic people of the Velay highlands around Le Puy, dependents of the Arverni.
vellavi.o: The Vellavi held the volcanic uplands of the upper Loire, in the modern Haute-Loire. Caesar lists them among the peoples under the authority of the Arverni.
vellavi.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Their territory lay on the routes from the Arverni lands south towards the Mediterranean.
vellavi.e: They followed the Arverni into the revolt of 52 BCE. Under Rome they formed a civitas with its chief town at Ruessium (Saint-Paulien), later moved to Anicium (Le Puy-en-Velay). Their name survives in the Velay.

voivodeship-of-litovoi.t: Romanian voivodeship west of the Olt whose ruler died fighting Hungary around 1279, an early step towards an independent Wallachia.
voivodeship-of-litovoi.o: Litovoi's land appears in Béla IV's charter of 1247 to the Knights Hospitaller, which names a knezate of Litovoi in the region of the Jiu and Olt, possibly including the Hațeg country across the Carpathians.
voivodeship-of-litovoi.r: Litovoi ruled Romanian knezes as a Hungarian tributary. A royal charter of 1285 says that around 1277–1279 a voivode Litovoi, with his brothers, seized part of the kingdom and refused to pay tribute to Ladislaus IV of Hungary.
voivodeship-of-litovoi.e: A Hungarian force under Master George defeated the rebels: Litovoi was killed and his brother Bărbat captured and forced to pay a large ransom. The land later became part of the Principality of Wallachia under Basarab I.

venetian-monemvasia.t: Venetian rule over the rock fortress of Monemvasia, the last free Byzantine town in the Peloponnese and home of malmsey wine.
venetian-monemvasia.o: Monemvasia, a fortified town on a rock island off the Laconian coast, belonged to the Despotate of the Morea. When Mehmed II conquered the Morea in 1460, the despot Thomas Palaiologos handed it to Pope Pius II. Papal rule proved weak, and in 1464 the inhabitants placed themselves under Venice.
venetian-monemvasia.r: Venetian officials governed with the town's Greek notables, maintaining its fortifications and port. Monemvasia, called Malvasia by the Italians, gave its name to malmsey, a sweet wine traded across Europe, although by this time most of it came from Crete. The town was largely cut off from its Ottoman-held hinterland.
venetian-monemvasia.e: In the peace of 1540 that ended the third Ottoman-Venetian war, Venice ceded Monemvasia and Nauplia to the Ottomans. It returned to Venetian control from 1690 to 1715 as part of the Venetian Morea.
